results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 57 outline summaries, written without the spec, match the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph, in the spec's order; no unit is unmatched.

Introduction ¶4 was marked as two ideas (normalizing layer / computed promise), but the spec paragraph p04 itself joins both halves of the chapter's two-part answer; the unit holds one idea, the claim.

How the Pieces Fit Together ¶6 was marked as two ideas (derived status / events stored per lane), but spec paragraph p17 itself declares 'two rules follow' from the vocabulary; the unit holds the spec's single joined idea.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim (S1 layer and choices, S2 booking and manifest, S3 event vocabulary and derived status, S4 computed promise, S5 measurement and staging) or is declared context, definition or transition in the spec; nothing needs to be cut or moved.

results.quote: | Promise service | Cut-off, backlog, stock location, lane table, performance margin | Most days including peak, if fed and measured | Events it has no data for yet |
results.finding: The how-the-promise-is-made table is followed directly by the next section heading; no sentence says what it shows (the spec: each step adds inputs and removes a blind spot). Every other table, figure and quotation is followed or framed by a sentence stating its point.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene: A Sentence in the Theme ¶5
results.quote: Waypoint, the company's improvement program, already requires availability and delivery dates through APIs in decision W8.
results.finding: The spec declares cause_effect carrying over the sentence's two failures (Eva, Black Friday) and introducing W8 as the decision that requires a computed answer instead. The paragraph opens on W8 with no reference to those failures, so the boundary does not say that the failures are why a computed answer is needed.

All other declared transitions are expressed at their boundaries, by an opening sentence or phrase (e.g. 'Two rules follow.', 'That scan history is half of what a computed promise needs.', 'The point for a newcomer is not the models.', 'What did not work was the promise', 'Noor's answer starts small.') or, for the comparison and failure lists, by bold labels and subheadings that carry the declared sequence or contrast; the hand-off links [[stores-and-omnichannel]].

Both flow readers describe the declared organising principle (problem, vocabulary, then the parcel's own order: label, tracking, then the promise that reads both, then choices, stages, evidence, failures) and mark every section's position clear or mostly clear.

results.quote: A computed one is an estimate with inputs, and the inputs are the chapter's argument.
results.finding: Both readers stalled on this sentence: it names no input, so the reader must wait for Figure 3 to learn what the inputs are. The order is fine; the sentence should list the inputs (order time, cut-off, backlog, stock location, lane transit, margin) as the spec's controlling idea does.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, section 3 item 7 ('This phrasing is odd and I had to re-read it')

results.finding: The introduction opens on the declared puzzling scenario (a shopper shown 'delivered tomorrow' after the last dispatch), then the carriers, Eva's parcel, the two-part answer and a roadmap; none of the weak patterns.

The conclusion opens by returning to the hook, sorts what holds into established, context-dependent and the author's synthesis, ends with questions and a hand-off; it does not open with 'in conclusion', add a new subtopic or end on a rephrased thesis alone.

What to Take Away ¶1 states what no single section states (the layer's events are the only lane record and the promise needs exactly that record, so the date is true only when the layer feeds a measured promise) and the so-what (start without a model: a transit table, cut-off and backlog, a weekly count per lane).
'Go back to the shopper who saw "delivered tomorrow" after the warehouse's last dispatch had left' returns to the hook named in callback.to and names the inputs and their sources.

The intro-only reader predicted the scene and request, the vocabulary, the three moments with options, cross-border and cost, the two four-way comparisons and scale, then public evidence, Eva's parcel and what goes wrong, and named the evidence (Kestrel & Pine's carriers and storefront text, carrier and vendor documentation, research on promises) and a plain practical tone; this matches the roadmap and the expected answer.

The reader gives Thursday, not Wednesday, because the order missed the 21:00 last wave so ships Wednesday plus one day transit; and names a computed promise from stock location, cut-off, backlog, lane transit and margin, measured promised-versus-delivered per lane, not reworded text. Matches the expected answer.

The reader names both faults and preventions: the retry booked a second shipment (two barcodes) for lack of the merchant's reference, prevented by an idempotent call by that reference with look-up before create; the batch was never manifested (a label is not a booking), prevented by a scheduled close-out with an alert and watching pre_transit. Matches the expected answer.

The reader derives the status from every carrier's scans mapped onto one small normalized vocabulary (lists the eight events), keeping the original event, never set by hand, read by page, notifications and agent alike, with each event stored with its lane. Matches the expected answer.
